newsitem.title: CHILE: Endesa joins Chile Atacama natgas project.
newsitem.headline: Endesa joins Chile Atacama natgas project.

text.p: Chile's largest power generator Empresa Nacional de Electricidad (Endesa) has joined a consortium planning to build a natural gas pipeline in north Chile, said an official from project leader CMS Energy Corp.

Asked if Endesa joined the project after the withdrawal of Canadian gas company NOVA Corp, CMS's Latin American representative Francisco Mezzadri said, "Effectively yes. The agreement with Nova was just an understanding."
Mezzadri said Endesa and CMS will own equal shares in the project with each expected to hold between 30 and 35 percent.
He was speaking at a ceremony attended by Economy Minster Alvaro Garcia to authorize foreign investment in the project.
The project involves building a natural gas-fired power plant with an initial capacity of 400 megawatts which will be increased to 600 megawatts in 2000, said Mezzadri.
An open season for natural gas producers to sign up pipeline capacity begins December 16 and continues through January 15, CMS said in a statement.
The total value of the project, including the power plant, is unchanged from the $700 million announced in September, CMS spokesman Kelly Farr said.
In the statement, CMS said both companies will have equal participation in the consortium, with the possible addition of Argentine natural gas producers as partners in the future.

"This is a project that will benefit Chile's Grand North area. In addition to providing competitively-priced electricity, it will also deliver natural gas to northern Chile's mining and industrial region, thereby stimulating economic growth," CMS said.
"Building a new power plant in Chile's copper mining region will diversify the area's coal-fired capacity with natural gas."
The 400-megawatt plant is scheduled to begin operation in 1999, with gas transportation from the pipeline expected to begin in February 1999, CMS said.

The 820-kilometer, 20-inch diameter Atacama Pipeline will originate in Argentina's Noroeste gas-producing basin, extending westward to Mejillones with the potential to extend laterals to Antofagasta, Tocopilla and Calama in northern Chile.
The pipeline will cost around $350 million, said Mezzadri.
CMS noted it and Endesa have been partners since 1993 in Hidroelectrica El Chocon, a 1,320-megawatt hydroelectric generating plant on the Limay River in western Argentina's Neuquen Province.
